sections.title: Walk the flowchart
sections.intro: kubectl answers instantly and everything already running is fine. But two different teammates report that "nothing new is happening." Figure out which component stopped.

questions.prompt: Existing pods are all Running and serving traffic, untouched. What does that already rule out?
options: kubelet and the node — they keep running pods alive
The scheduler — it would evict running pods
Nothing yet — every component is still a suspect
The controller-manager — it restarts running pods
questions.explanation: Neither the scheduler nor the controller-manager is needed to keep a running pod alive, so a healthy steady state is exactly what you'd expect if one of them died. The fact that only new things are broken is the clue.

questions.prompt: Both components fit "nothing automatic is happening." What's the question that actually tells them apart?
options: Which kube-system pod has the most restarts?
Is it one namespace, or every namespace?
Is etcd slow to persist new objects?
New pods not *placed*, or missing pods not *replaced*?
questions.explanation: The scheduler owns placement: binding a pod to a node. The controller-manager owns reconciliation: noticing that desired state ≠ actual state and creating objects to close the gap. Which side of the lifecycle is stuck tells you which one is down.

questions.prompt: You want a test you can run without harming anything real. Which is best?
options: Cordon a node and see whether pods move
Delete a production pod and watch for a replacement
Restart both components and see which fixes it
Create a throwaway Deployment and see how far it gets
questions.explanation: A throwaway Deployment goes through both components in order. The Deployment controller has to create a ReplicaSet and a pod (controller-manager), then the scheduler has to bind that pod. Where it stops tells you which one is broken. Restarting both might fix it, but you'd learn nothing.

questions.prompt: Result of the test. Which component is down?
questions.snippet:
$ kubectl get rs,pods -l app=probe
No resources found in default namespace.

$ kubectl get deployment probe
NAME    READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
probe   0/1     0            0           2m
options: The scheduler — the pod can't be placed
etcd — the objects weren't saved
kubelet — the node never started the pod
The controller-manager — no ReplicaSet was ever created
questions.explanation: The scheduler can only place a pod that exists. Here no pod object exists at all, because the reconcile loop never turned the Deployment into a ReplicaSet. etcd is fine: the Deployment itself was saved and read back.

questions.prompt: You confirm it. What's the real cost of this outage, beyond the fix itself?
questions.snippet:
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep controller-manager
kube-controller-manager-cp-1   0/1   CrashLoopBackOff   7   12m
options: Every reconcile loop is paused — drift piles up
etcd will lose data written meanwhile
Running pods will start crashing soon
None — running pods are completely unaffected
questions.explanation: The fix is just restarting the static pod and reading its logs for why it crashed. What matters is the window: nothing self-heals while it's down, so duration matters more than the fix.

questions.prompt: Rerun the same test on a different cluster. Now which is it?
questions.snippet:
$ kubectl get rs,pods -l app=probe
NAME                       DESIRED   CURRENT   READY
replicaset.apps/probe-7c   1         1         0

NAME           READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
pod/probe-7c-x   0/1     Pending   0          3m

$ kubectl describe pod probe-7c-x | tail -1
Events:  <none>
options: The controller-manager — the pod isn't running
The scheduler — the pod exists but nothing placed it
The image — it can't be pulled
Capacity — the cluster is full
questions.explanation: A resource shortage would leave a FailedScheduling event explaining why. Zero events means the scheduler never attempted it. If every new pod looks like this, check `kube-scheduler` in `kube-system`.

questions.prompt: This is an HA control plane: three nodes, and all three `kube-scheduler` pods show Running. But pods still aren't being placed. What do you check?
options: kube-proxy logs on each control-plane node
The leader-election lease and its `renewTime`
`etcdctl member list` on each node
Nothing — Running means the scheduler is fine
questions.explanation: Only one replica does the work. A pod showing Running proves the process exists, not that it's doing anything useful. The lease shows who's supposed to be working and when it last checked in.

questions.prompt: Final sanity check: someone reports "I deleted a pod from the `reports` Deployment and nothing replaced it." Before blaming the controller-manager, what do you look at?
options: etcd health on the control plane
kubelet logs on the pod's old node
The Deployment's desired replica count
The scheduler logs in kube-system
questions.explanation: No replacement is only a failure if something wanted one. Confirm the desired state before calling it broken.

questions.prompt: A pod sits Pending with this event. Is the scheduler broken?
questions.snippet: Warning  FailedScheduling  default-scheduler  0/4 nodes are available: 4 Insufficient cpu.
options: Yes — a failed schedule means it's broken
Yes — restart it to clear the queue
No — it's working; it's telling you the constraint
No — it's the controller-manager's fault
questions.explanation: Getting a FailedScheduling event at all proves the scheduler is alive and doing its job. "Scheduler down" looks like silence, not a complaint.

questions.prompt: Namespaces stay stuck in `Terminating` forever, and Service Endpoints don't update when pods come and go. One component explains both. Which?
options: The controller-manager — both loops live inside it
CoreDNS — it tracks namespace state
The scheduler — it places Endpoints too
kube-proxy — it owns Endpoints and namespaces
questions.explanation: The controller-manager is many reconcile loops bundled into one process. When it dies, every loop stops at once, so symptoms that look unrelated across the cluster are a strong hint.

questions.prompt: Under heavy load, an HPA never adds replicas. Is this the controller-manager core loop failing?
options: Yes — the ReplicaSet controller is down
Probably not — check the HPA's metrics source first
No — it's the scheduler not placing pods
Yes — etcd isn't storing the new count
questions.explanation: The HPA controller runs in the controller-manager, but its usual failure is missing input, not a dead loop. If deleted pods still get replaced, the core reconciliation is fine and only the metrics pipeline is broken.

questions.prompt: On a managed cluster (EKS/GKE), `kubectl get pods -n kube-system` shows no scheduler or controller-manager pods at all. Are they down?
options: Yes — they were deleted and need reinstalling
Yes — managed clusters still show them
No — managed clusters don't have a scheduler
Not necessarily — the provider hides the control plane
questions.explanation: Not seeing them is normal on managed Kubernetes. The placement-vs-replacement test still works because it only uses the API.

questions.prompt: You see this. What does it say about cluster behavior right now?
questions.snippet:
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep scheduler
kube-scheduler-cp-1   0/1   CrashLoopBackOff   6   10m
options: Running pods are being evicted from nodes
New pods won't be placed; running pods are fine
kubectl will stop responding shortly
Deleted pods won't get replacement objects
questions.explanation: Replacement pod *objects* will still be created, because the controller-manager is fine. They'll just pile up in Pending with no events until the scheduler is back.
